This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building canary releases — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary canary releases tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Validate canary releases outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
2. Surface known limitations of a chosen canary releases approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
3. Measure before optimizing any canary releases bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
4. Keep canary releases changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
5. Before starting canary releases work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
6. State assumptions about canary releases explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
7. When multiple canary releases strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. Keep canary releases outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic canary releases advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new canary releases abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not skip documenting canary releases assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid mixing unrelated canary releases concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not silently drop canary releases edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for canary releases, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
